title: Pricing by hours per project for Medical equipment cleaning (external only)
audience: Owners and supervisors who quote external cleaning of medical equipment and furniture under a facility's written instruction, and who need a price that covers cost, release and checking time and earns a margin.
learningOutcomes: Calculate a cost per productive hour from the owner's own figures, including training, PPE and equipment-handling time
Estimate hours for a batch of named items, including collection, travel, set-up and checking
Build a quote from hours, a rate and a margin, with scope, exclusions and the facility's inputs stated

instruction.heading: Why hours are the starting unit
instruction.body: External equipment work comes in batches: a list of trolleys, cabinets and chairs for a set window. Hours make visible the time to collect and return items, set-up, the cleaning itself, checking and sign-off. The sample business plan that the base lesson draws on is not a medical-equipment source, so no figure is taken from it. A flat price without hours cannot be defended when a facility asks why a batch costs what it does.

instruction.heading: Build the cost per productive hour
instruction.body: Take the total cost of running the business over a period and divide it by the chargeable hours in that period. Total cost includes wages with the on-costs your staff arrangements require, such as leave and superannuation (business.gov.au, 1 October 2026), along with vehicle running costs, equipment, consumables, PPE, training, insurance, administration and premises. Chargeable hours are the hours spent on billable work, not paid roster time. Billable time is often about 60 to 80 per cent of working hours, a general range from Jobber rather than an Australian figure. The cleaning award rates were not retrieved for this course, so confirm which award or enterprise agreement applies to each worker before using any cost figure.

instruction.heading: Estimate the hours by item
instruction.body: List every item on the facility's written list, group the items by type (for example, trolleys, bed frames, cabinets and chairs), and estimate each type at a standard speed. Add collection and return, travel between rooms, set-up, checking and sign-off as named lines. Add an allowance for delays outside your control, such as a late release of an item by the clinic. A general service guide suggests adding 10 to 20 per cent to job estimates for unexpected work (Xero Australia, 3 September 2026). That is a general range, so set your own allowance from your records. After each batch, record the actual hours and the reason for any difference.

instruction.heading: Turn hours into a price
instruction.body: Multiply the crew hours by the cost per productive hour and add the delay allowance. Then add a margin for the risk in the batch, such as a release that depends on clinical staff or a tight window between sessions. Apply your consumables and PPE policy and any minimum charge. Show the basis of the price, so that the facility can see which items and hours it is paying for.

instruction.heading: Keep the quote honest
instruction.body: State the item list, the surfaces, the hours or price basis, the exclusions (critical or semi-critical equipment, reprocessing of reusable devices, internal devices), the facility's inputs (list, release and access) and how long the quote is valid. Re-quote any change to the list before the work starts.

instruction.heading: Review your estimates
instruction.body: Compare estimated and actual hours for at least the first ten batches, and review the variance monthly. If the variance is consistently above an agreed threshold, change the standard time, the allowance or the scope rules. The method is finished only when actual hours match quoted hours closely enough for the work to make money.

procedure: Gather the year's total business costs, including PPE and training, and the chargeable hours in the same period.
Divide total costs by chargeable hours to get the cost per productive hour, and date the worksheet.
Group the facility's items by type, and estimate each type's time as a range.
Add collection, return, travel, set-up, checking and sign-off as named lines.
Add the delay allowance, multiply crew hours by the cost per productive hour, then apply the margin.
Apply the consumables and PPE policy and the minimum charge.
Write the quote with item scope, hours basis, exclusions, facility inputs and validity.
Record actual hours after each batch and compare them with the estimate.

workedExamples.situation: Illustrative figures only, not medical-equipment rates. A clinic asks for external cleaning of 12 trolleys, 4 cabinets and 6 chairs in one session. The estimate is 5 crew-hours, including collection, set-up, checking and sign-off. The placeholder cost per productive hour is $60 AUD. A 10 per cent delay allowance is added, at the low end of the general 10 to 20 per cent range. The target margin on price is 25 per cent (illustrative).
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What is the cost, what is the price, and what changes if the clinic cannot release the trolleys until an hour after the window opens?
workedExamples.reasoning: Five crew-hours at $60 AUD is $300 AUD, and a 10 per cent allowance adds $30 AUD, so the cost is $330 AUD. A 25 per cent margin on price gives $440 AUD, because the price is the cost divided by 0.75. If the late release adds an hour, the crew hours become six, the cost becomes $396 AUD and the price becomes $528 AUD, but only if the quote lets that time be charged. The owner checks those terms first. The research found no medical-equipment pricing, so the $60 figure is a placeholder to be replaced with the owner's own cost.

Facility's written item list for each batch

commonErrors.error: Pricing from the hourly wage alone
commonErrors.prevention: Include on-costs, PPE, training, vehicle, equipment, consumables, insurance and administration in the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Counting paid hours as productive hours
commonErrors.prevention: Use chargeable hours only when calculating the cost per productive hour.

commonErrors.error: Leaving out collection, release and checking time
commonErrors.prevention: Add these as named lines on every estimate.
List exclusions, including reprocessing and critical equipment, what the facility provides, and the access assumptions.

commonErrors.error: Never comparing estimates with actual hours
commonErrors.prevention: Record actual hours after each batch and review the variance monthly.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: This is pricing guidance only. The Australian Consumer Law applies to pricing statements, and misleading statements about prices are prohibited (ACCC, 15 July 2026). State or territory fair trading rules also apply. This lesson gives no medical-equipment rate, because the research did not find one.

Pay rates, allowances and on-costs for employees may be set by an award or enterprise agreement. The cleaning award rates were not retrieved for this course. Check the instrument that applies to each worker before using any cost figure.

qualityStandard: Each quote shows item scope, hours or price basis, exclusions, facility inputs and validity.
The cost per productive hour is calculated from the owner's own records and dated.
Actual hours are recorded for at least the first ten batches and compared with the estimate.
No quote is issued without a margin decision and a minimum-charge check.
documentationEvidence: Cost per productive hour worksheet, dated, with the source of each figure
Quote showing item scope, hours basis, exclusions and validity
Batch time log with estimated and actual hours
summary: Hours make the batch visible, so start every quote from the item list and the hours.
Cost per productive hour uses chargeable time, not paid time.
Collection, release and checking time are named lines, not hidden extras.
Compare estimates with actual hours, and change the method when they diverge.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which costs belong in the cost per productive hour for an external equipment cleaning business?
options: Only the hourly wage of the lowest-paid worker and nothing else from the accounts or the rent
The price the client pays, plus the deposit, the late fee and the crew bonus paid
The average hourly rate of competitors in the local area and their fees for the whole year
Wages with on-costs, vehicle, equipment, consumables, insurance and administration, divided by chargeable hours

knowledgeChecks.question: A batch is estimated at 5 crew-hours and takes 8. What is the right response?
options: Record the actual hours, find the cause, and adjust the estimate and future quotes
Leave the estimate, since the client has already paid and the crew has finished
Reduce paid hours for the crew on the next job and skip the morning break
Raise the price for this client's next job only and no one else is charged more

knowledgeChecks.question: Why does a quote need an exclusions list?
options: To hide the margin from the client and to keep the rates a secret from the crew
To make the quote longer and to fill up the page with more text and words for the client
To show what the price covers, so scope changes can be priced and disputes are reduced
To lower the client's expectations and to make the job seem much smaller than it is
